title: The Abbasid Caliphate
subtitle: 750–945 · Baghdad, the Translation Movement and the House of Islam

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The Abbasid caliphs — from the founding of Baghdad to the day the Buyids walked in

entries.label: Al-Mansur founds Baghdad
entries.hint: Al-Mansur consolidated the new dynasty by killing its own kingmaker, Abu Muslim, and in 762 laid out a perfectly circular administrative capital on the Tigris near the ruins of Ctesiphon. The move announced what the Abbasid state would be: Iraqi, Persian-influenced, and built around the caliph.
entries.note: al-Tabari; al-Ya'qubi's description of Baghdad; Lassner, 'The Shaping of Abbasid Rule' (1980); Kennedy, 'When Baghdad Ruled the Muslim World' (2004).

entries.label: Harun al-Rashid and the Barmakids
entries.hint: Harun's reign became the golden age of legend — the wealth, the annual pilgrimage or campaign, the embassy exchange with Charlemagne. Much of the governing was done by the Barmakid family of viziers until Harun destroyed them in 803, in a purge that has never been fully explained.
entries.note: al-Tabari; the Barmakids (Bouvat; van Bladel); the 'Thousand and One Nights' frame as later legend, not evidence.

entries.label: The war between al-Amin and al-Ma'mun
entries.hint: Harun divided the succession between two sons and they went to war. Al-Ma'mun's Khurasani army besieged and stormed Baghdad in 813, killing al-Amin. Al-Ma'mun then ruled from Merv for six years before returning — and the balance of the empire tilted decisively toward its Iranian east.
entries.note: al-Tabari; the siege of Baghdad (the poet's lament of al-Khuraymi); Cooperson, 'Al-Ma'mun' (2005).

entries.label: Al-Ma'mun — the mihna and the House of Wisdom
entries.hint: Al-Ma'mun sponsored the translation of Greek science on a grand scale, briefly named a Shia imam as his heir, and in his last months imposed the doctrine of the created Quran on the scholars by inquisition (the mihna). He tried to make the caliph the arbiter of doctrine, and failed.
entries.note: al-Tabari; the mihna edicts (see Order); Cooperson (2005); Gutas, 'Greek Thought, Arabic Culture' (1998).

entries.label: Al-Mu'tasim, Samarra and the Turkish soldiers
entries.loc: Samarra, on the Tigris north of Baghdad
entries.hint: Al-Mu'tasim built a personal army of enslaved Turkish cavalry (ghilman) and, when Baghdad resented them, moved the whole government 125 km upriver to a new city, Samarra. It solved one problem and created a worse one: an army loyal to its commanders, not the dynasty.
entries.note: al-Tabari; Gordon, 'The Breaking of a Thousand Swords: A History of the Turkish Military of Samarra' (2001); Northedge, 'The Historical Topography of Samarra' (2005).

entries.label: The Samarra anarchy and the slide to 945
entries.hint: Between 861 and 870 the Turkish troops made and murdered four caliphs. A partial recovery under al-Mu'tadid brought the court back to Baghdad, but by al-Muqtadir's reign (908–932) the treasury was empty, the provinces were gone, and in 945 the Buyids simply occupied the capital and kept the caliph as a pensioner.
entries.note: al-Tabari and Miskawayh, 'Tajarib al-Umam'; Bonner, 'The Waning of Empire, 861–945', in the New Cambridge History of Islam vol. 1 (2010).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The storming of Baghdad, two decades of Khurramite revolt, the Byzantine war, and the Zanj at the gates

entries.label: The siege of Baghdad
entries.hint: Al-Ma'mun's general Tahir blockaded the capital for over a year; catapults wrecked the palaces and the round city, and the fighting in the streets was remembered in a famous poem of lament. The first Abbasid civil war left the dynasty's own capital in ruins.
entries.note: al-Tabari; al-Khuraymi's elegy for Baghdad; Cooperson, 'Al-Ma'mun' (2005).

entries.label: Babak and the Khurramite revolt
entries.hint: Babak led a rural revolt in the mountains of Azerbaijan under a religion mixing older Iranian traditions with social radicalism. It defeated Abbasid army after Abbasid army for twenty years and tied down the caliphate's forces until al-Mu'tasim's Turkish troops finally crushed it in 837.
entries.note: al-Tabari; the Khurramiyya (Crone, 'The Nativist Prophets of Early Islamic Iran', 2012).

entries.label: The sack of Amorion and the turning of the tide
entries.hint: Al-Mu'tasim's storming of Amorion in 838 was the last great Abbasid victory over Byzantium. A generation later, at Lalakaon in 863, a Byzantine army destroyed the emir of Melitene, and the frontier began its long shift the other way — toward the Byzantine reconquests of the 960s.
entries.note: al-Tabari; Theophanes Continuatus; the '42 Martyrs of Amorion'; Treadgold, 'A History of the Byzantine State and Society' (1997).

entries.label: The Zanj Revolt reaches toward Baghdad
entries.hint: The rising of the enslaved East African labourers of the salt flats built a state in the southern marshes, sacked Basra, minted coins and held out for fourteen years, coming within eighty kilometres of Baghdad. It absorbed the caliphate's whole military effort in the decade its provinces were breaking away.
entries.note: al-Tabari's detailed account; Popovic, 'The Revolt of African Slaves in Iraq' (1999). Cross-references the Islamic Eastern Arabia folio.

entries.label: Ya'qub the Coppersmith marches on Baghdad
entries.loc: Dayr al-Aqul, on the Tigris below Baghdad
entries.hint: Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar rose from a coppersmith's apprentice to rule Sistan, Khurasan and Fars, then marched on the capital itself in 876. He was beaten fifty miles short of Baghdad, but a provincial adventurer had come closer to taking the caliphate than anyone since the revolution.
entries.note: al-Tabari; the Saffarids (Bosworth, 'The History of the Saffarids of Sistan', 1994).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: A planned capital, the vizierate, the inquisition of the created Quran, and a state that ran out of money

entries.label: The vizierate and the diwans
entries.hint: The Abbasids revived the Sasanian model: a wazir as head of government (the Barmakids made the office), a set of specialised bureaus (kharaj for tax, jund for the army, rasa'il for correspondence, barid for post and intelligence), and a large professional secretary class, the kuttab, most of them of Persian background.
entries.note: al-Jahshiyari, 'Kitab al-Wuzara wa'l-Kuttab'; Kennedy, 'The Court of the Caliphs' (2004); the Sasanian administrative inheritance.

entries.label: The mihna — the inquisition of the created Quran
entries.hint: Al-Ma'mun and his two successors required judges, witnesses and scholars to profess that the Quran was created, not eternal — a Mu'tazili position — and imprisoned those who refused. Ahmad ibn Hanbal's public resistance made him a hero; al-Mutawakkil abandoned the policy in 849. The caliph never again claimed to define dogma.
entries.note: al-Tabari; the mihna edicts translated in Patton, 'Ahmad ibn Hanbal and the Mihna' (1897); Nawas and Cooperson on its politics.

entries.label: The theory of the caliphate is written down
entries.hint: As the caliph's real power drained away, jurists began to define what the office was: a communal obligation to appoint one imam, from Quraysh, to lead prayer, war and justice and enforce the law. The gap between this ideal and the pensioner in the Baghdad palace shaped Islamic political thought for centuries.
entries.note: the pre-Mawardi juristic material (Crone, 'Medieval Islamic Political Thought', 2004); al-Mawardi's 'Ahkam al-Sultaniyya' comes just after this folio (1045).

entries.label: The iqta and the fiscal collapse
entries.hint: Unable to pay the army in cash, the government began assigning soldiers and officials the revenue of estates and districts directly (iqta). It kept the troops fed and hollowed out the central treasury at the same time. By 945 the caliph could not fund a bodyguard.
entries.note: Miskawayh, 'Tajarib al-Umam'; the fiscal crisis under al-Muqtadir (van Berkel et al., 'Crisis and Continuity at the Abbasid Court', 2013).

entries.label: Al-Mutawakkil's edicts on the dhimmis
entries.hint: Al-Mutawakkil ordered non-Muslims to wear distinctive dress and honey-coloured patches, barred them from state office, and had recently built churches and synagogues demolished. Enforcement was uneven and often lapsed, but the edicts fixed a template of legal subordination that later rulers could revive.
entries.note: al-Tabari, s.a. 235 and 239 AH; Levy-Rubin, 'Non-Muslims in the Early Islamic Empire' (2011).

entries.label: The barid as the caliph's eyes
entries.loc: the trunk roads of the empire
entries.hint: The postmaster of each province reported directly and secretly to the caliph on the conduct of the governor, the state of the crops, and the price of bread. The barid was as much an intelligence service as a mail system, and its route-books became the first Arabic administrative geography.
entries.note: Ibn Khordadbeh, 'Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik' (himself a postmaster); Silverstein, 'Postal Systems in the Pre-Modern Islamic World' (2007).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The law schools, the hadith canon, rational theology and its defeat, the Occultation, and Sufism

entries.label: The four Sunni schools of law take shape
entries.hint: Abu Hanifa's circle in Kufa, Malik's in Medina (his Muwatta), al-Shafi'i (whose Risala founded the theory of the four sources of law), and Ahmad ibn Hanbal's hadith-first school in Baghdad hardened into the four enduring Sunni madhhabs over this century.
entries.note: Malik, 'al-Muwatta'; al-Shafi'i, 'al-Risala'; Hallaq, 'The Origins and Evolution of Islamic Law' (2005); Melchert, 'The Formation of the Sunni Schools of Law' (1997).

entries.label: Al-Bukhari, Muslim and the canon of hadith
entries.hint: Al-Bukhari (d. 870) and Muslim (d. 875) sifted hundreds of thousands of reported sayings of the Prophet down to a few thousand judged sound, organised by legal topic. Their two 'Sahih' collections, with four others, became the canonical Sunni hadith corpus and the science of authenticating transmitters matured around them.
entries.note: the 'Kutub al-Sitta'; Brown, 'The Canonization of al-Bukhari and Muslim' (2007).

entries.label: The Mu'tazila and rational theology
entries.hint: The Mu'tazila built a systematic theology on reason: God's absolute unity (which made the Quran a created thing) and God's justice (which made humans the free authors of their acts). Backed by al-Ma'mun and enforced in the mihna, the school lost state protection under al-Mutawakkil and slowly declined.
entries.note: the Mu'tazili 'five principles'; Abd al-Jabbar's later 'Mughni' preserves the system; van Ess, 'Theologie und Gesellschaft' (1991–97).

entries.label: Al-Ash'ari and the Sunni theological settlement
entries.hint: Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, trained as a Mu'tazili, broke with the school around 912 and used its own rational methods to defend the traditionalist positions — an eternal Quran, God's attributes real but unknowable, acts created by God and 'acquired' by man. Ash'arism became the dominant Sunni kalam.
entries.note: al-Ash'ari, 'al-Ibana' and 'Maqalat al-Islamiyyin'; the parallel Maturidi school in Samarqand; Watt, 'The Formative Period of Islamic Thought' (1973).

entries.label: The line of imams ends — the Occultation
entries.hint: When the eleventh imam died in Samarra in 874 leaving no visible heir, his followers held that a son existed in hiding and communicated through four successive agents. When the last agent died in 941 without naming a successor, the 'Greater Occultation' began, and Twelver Shiism became a community awaiting a hidden imam.
entries.note: al-Kulayni, 'al-Kafi' (d. 941); Hussain, 'The Occultation of the Twelfth Imam' (1982); Modarressi, 'Crisis and Consolidation in the Formative Period of Shi'ite Islam' (1993).

entries.label: The Ismaili da'wa and a third caliphate
entries.hint: A clandestine missionary movement expecting the return of a hidden Ismaili imam spread from Syria across the Maghreb, Yemen, Sind and eastern Arabia (where it produced the Qarmatian state). In 909 its leader emerged in Tunisia and was proclaimed the Fatimid caliph — the third simultaneous claimant to the office.
entries.note: Daftary, 'The Ismailis: Their History and Doctrines' (2nd ed. 2007); Halm, 'The Empire of the Mahdi' (1996). Continued in a future Fatimid folio; cross-references the Qarmatian entries.

entries.label: Sufism takes form — al-Junayd and al-Hallaj
entries.hint: Baghdad became the centre of a self-conscious mystical movement: al-Muhasibi's spiritual self-examination, al-Junayd's 'sober' path of union-then-return, and al-Hallaj, executed in the city in 922 after saying 'I am the Truth' — the mystic's claim of annihilation in God read as blasphemy, and as a challenge to the scholars' monopoly on religious authority.
entries.note: al-Sarraj, 'Kitab al-Luma'; Massignon, 'The Passion of al-Hallaj' (1922/1982); Karamustafa, 'Sufism: The Formative Period' (2007).

entries.label: The geonim, Saadia Gaon and the Karaite schism
entries.loc: the academies of Sura and Pumbedita, near Baghdad
entries.hint: The heads (geonim) of the Babylonian rabbinic academies were the supreme authorities for Jews across the Islamic world and beyond, ruling by responsa. Saadia Gaon (d. 942) translated the Bible into Arabic and wrote the first Jewish systematic theology; against him and the rabbis stood the scripturalist Karaites, who rejected the Talmud entirely.
entries.note: Saadia Gaon, 'Kitab al-Amanat wa'l-I'tiqadat'; the geonic responsa; the Karaite–Rabbanite split (Rustow, 'Heresy and the Politics of Community', 2008).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Samarra and its spiral minaret, the paper book, adab prose, and the poetry of the moderns

entries.label: Samarra and the spiral minaret
entries.hint: For fifty-six years the caliphate governed from a strip city forty kilometres long on the Tigris. Its Great Mosque was the largest in the world, fronted by a free-standing spiral ramp-minaret (the Malwiya); its palaces sprawled over racecourses and game reserves; and it was abandoned so completely that its plan survives almost intact.
entries.note: Northedge, 'The Historical Topography of Samarra' (2005); Samarra is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2007).

entries.label: The Samarra stucco style spreads the empire over
entries.hint: Samarra's palace decorators developed a moulded stucco of endlessly repeating abstract, slant-cut vegetal forms — the 'beveled style' — that could be cast in quantity. Carried by craftsmen and imitation, it turns up from Egypt to Central Asia and is the first empire-wide Islamic ornamental language.
entries.note: Herzfeld's Samarra excavations; the 'Style C' / beveled style and its diffusion (Ettinghausen & Grabar, 'The Art and Architecture of Islam 650–1250').

entries.label: Paper, the warraqs and the book trade
entries.hint: A paper mill was working in Baghdad by the 790s, and within a lifetime cheap paper had displaced papyrus and parchment for everyday use. A whole trade of stationer-copyists (warraqun) grew up around the mosque; books multiplied, and with them the possibility of private libraries and mass scholarship.
entries.note: Bloom, 'Paper Before Print' (2001); the warraq trade (Toorawa, 'Ibn Abi Tahir Tayfur and Arabic Writerly Culture', 2005).

entries.label: Adab prose — al-Jahiz and the translated wisdom
entries.hint: Ibn al-Muqaffa turned the Persian mirror-for-princes and the Indian animal fables (Kalila wa Dimna) into Arabic before his execution around 756. Al-Jahiz then made Arabic prose into an instrument for everything — zoology, theology, misers, the singing-girls, the superiority of blacks — in a witty, digressive style that founded the genre of adab.
entries.note: al-Jahiz, 'Kitab al-Hayawan', 'Kitab al-Bukhala', 'al-Bayan wa'l-Tabyin'; Ibn al-Muqaffa, 'Kalila wa Dimna'; Pellat, 'The Life and Works of Jahiz' (1969).

entries.label: The poetry of the 'moderns'
entries.hint: A generation of poets broke with the desert conventions of the ode: Abu Nuwas made wine and the love of boys his subject and mocked the Bedouin nostalgia; Abu Tammam and al-Buhturi pursued dense rhetorical figures; Ibn al-Rumi wrote long psychological portraits. Arabic poetry became urban, personal and self-aware.
entries.note: the muhdathun; Abu Nuwas, Diwan; Abu Tammam's 'Hamasa' anthology; the debate over 'new' vs 'old' style (Ibn Qutayba's introduction to 'al-Shi'r wa'l-Shu'ara').

entries.label: The classical and the romantic schools of song
entries.hint: The Abbasid court sustained a full art-music culture around the singing-girls and the master singers. Ishaq al-Mawsili defended a 'classical' fidelity to the old repertoire against the caliph's brother Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi, who sang in a freer, more ornamented style. It is the first documented debate about musical authenticity.
entries.note: Kitab al-Aghani (al-Isfahani, mid-10th c., the essential source); Sawa, 'Music Performance Practice in the Early Abbasid Era 132–320 AH' (1989).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Greek sciences enter Arabic; algebra, the numerals, clinical medicine, the size of the Earth

entries.label: The Translation Movement
entries.hint: Over two centuries, sustained by caliphs, viziers and private patrons, nearly the entire surviving corpus of Greek philosophy, medicine, mathematics and astronomy was translated into Arabic, mostly through Syriac and mostly by Christian scholars. Hunayn ibn Ishaq's school set the standard for accuracy. No comparable transfer of knowledge had happened before.
entries.note: Gutas, 'Greek Thought, Arabic Culture: The Graeco-Arabic Translation Movement in Baghdad' (1998); the 'Bayt al-Hikma' as a translation bureau, not a research academy (Gutas's corrective).

entries.label: Al-Khwarizmi — algebra and the numerals
entries.hint: Al-Khwarizmi's book on 'restoration and balancing' (al-jabr) founded algebra as a discipline; another work introduced the Indian decimal place-value numerals and the use of zero to the Arabic-reading world. His name, Latinised, became 'algorithm', and his numerals became ours.
entries.note: al-Khwarizmi, 'al-Kitab al-Mukhtasar fi Hisab al-Jabr wa'l-Muqabala' and the lost arithmetic surviving in Latin ('Algoritmi de numero Indorum').

entries.label: Al-Kindi — the philosopher of the Arabs
entries.hint: Al-Kindi supervised translations, argued that philosophy and revelation reach the same truth, and wrote on metaphysics, optics, medicine, music and — founding the field — the cryptanalytic technique of frequency analysis. He made falsafa, Greek-derived philosophy, a permanent presence in Arabic thought.
entries.note: al-Kindi, 'On First Philosophy'; Adamson, 'Al-Kindi' (2007); the 'Risala on Deciphering Cryptographic Messages'.

entries.label: Al-Razi and the Baghdad hospital
entries.hint: Al-Razi (Rhazes) directed hospitals at Rayy and Baghdad, kept detailed case notes, wrote the first clinical description distinguishing smallpox from measles, and compiled the vast 'Comprehensive Book' of medicine. He also argued, in works that shocked his contemporaries, that prophecy was unnecessary and reason sufficient.
entries.note: al-Razi, 'Kitab al-Hawi' and 'al-Judari wa'l-Hasba'; the bimaristan as an institution (Pormann & Savage-Smith, 'Medieval Islamic Medicine', 2007).

entries.label: Al-Ma'mun measures the Earth
entries.loc: the Sinjar plain, northern Iraq; observatories at Baghdad and Damascus
entries.hint: Al-Ma'mun had teams pace out a degree of latitude on the flat Sinjar plain to check the size of the Earth, and set up observatories to correct Ptolemy's star positions. The resulting 'Verified Tables' (al-Zij al-Mumtahan) began the Arabic tradition of observational astronomy.
entries.note: the degree measurement (al-Biruni's later account); the Mumtahan zij; King & Saliba on early Islamic astronomy.

entries.label: History and geography become disciplines
entries.hint: Al-Baladhuri wrote the conquests, Ibn Khordadbeh the roads and revenues of the empire, al-Ya'qubi a universal history and geography, al-Tabari a year-by-year history of the world from creation, and al-Masudi a discursive survey of everything. Prose history and descriptive geography reached maturity together.
entries.note: al-Tabari, 'Tarikh'; al-Masudi, 'Muruj al-Dhahab'; Ibn Khordadbeh, 'al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik'; Robinson, 'Islamic Historiography' (2003).

entries.label: The Brethren of Purity
entries.hint: An anonymous group in Basra produced the 'Epistles of the Brethren of Purity', a 52-part encyclopedia covering mathematics, logic, natural science, psychology and theology in a Neoplatonic and Ismaili-tinged synthesis meant to purify the soul. It was one of the most widely copied works of the medieval Islamic world.
entries.note: 'Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa'; el-Bizri (ed.), 'The Ikhwan al-Safa and their Rasa'il' (2008).
keywords: Epistles of the Brethren of Purity

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The largest city west of China, banking instruments, the Indian Ocean apogee, and a bankrupt treasury

entries.label: Baghdad and the instruments of finance
entries.hint: Baghdad may have held close to a million people by 900, the largest city outside China. Its money-changers (sarrafun) developed a real banking system — deposit accounts, the transfer order (the 'sakk', origin of 'cheque'), and the long-distance bill of exchange (suftaja) that let a merchant deposit cash in Baghdad and draw it in Cairo.
entries.note: Fischel, 'Jews in the Economic and Political Life of Mediaeval Islam' (1937); Udovitch, 'Partnership and Profit in Medieval Islam' (1970).

entries.label: The Indian Ocean trade at its height
entries.loc: Basra, Siraf, the Gulf; to India, Malaya and China
entries.hint: Baghdad's demand pulled the western Indian Ocean into its most intense phase of long-distance trade — dhows sailing from the Gulf ports to Guangzhou for silk and porcelain, to East Africa for gold and slaves, to India for pepper and teak. The 'age of Sindbad' was the caliphate's commercial hinterland.
entries.note: the 'Akhbar al-Sin wa'l-Hind'; Chaudhuri, 'Trade and Civilisation in the Indian Ocean' (1985). Cross-references the Gulf folios.

entries.label: The Sawad — the granary and its decline
entries.hint: The irrigated land between the Tigris and Euphrates was the caliphate's single largest revenue source. Over the folio's span its yield fell — from over-taxation, the neglect of the canal grid, the salinisation of the soil, and the devastation of the Zanj war — and the decline of the Sawad was the decline of the Abbasid state.
entries.note: the land-tax figures in the fiscal manuals (Qudama ibn Ja'far; Ibn Khordadbeh); Waines, 'The Third Century Internal Crisis of the Abbasids', JESHO (1977).

entries.label: The treasury goes bankrupt
entries.hint: Under al-Muqtadir the government's spending — an enormous court, an unpayable army, provincial revolts — outran a revenue base that the provinces were no longer remitting. Viziers were appointed and imprisoned for the money they could raise; the coinage was debased; and by 945 the caliph was insolvent.
entries.note: Miskawayh, 'Tajarib al-Umam'; van Berkel et al., 'Crisis and Continuity at the Abbasid Court' (2013).

entries.label: The dirham flows north — the Rus trade
entries.hint: Hundreds of thousands of Abbasid and Samanid silver dirhams have been dug up in Russia, the Baltic and Scandinavia — payment for the furs, amber, honey and, above all, slaves that the Rus and the Volga Bulgars traded south. The caliphate's silver funded the Viking-age economy of northern Europe.
entries.note: the dirham hoards (Noonan's studies); Ibn Fadlan's 921–922 embassy to the Volga Bulgars.

entries.label: The paper and sugar industries
entries.hint: Two new manufacturing industries scaled up under the caliphate: paper, made from rag and initially concentrated in Baghdad and Samarqand, and cane sugar, refined in Khuzistan and Egypt with hydraulic mills. Both were export goods and both would later travel west to Europe.
entries.note: Bloom, 'Paper Before Print' (2001); Ouerfelli, 'Le sucre' (2008) on the medieval sugar industry.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Paper, ingenious devices, the astrolabe workshop, and the hospital as an institution

entries.label: The paper technology transfer
entries.hint: Paper-making — a Chinese technique, said to have been learned from prisoners taken at Talas in 751 — was established at Samarqand and then Baghdad, adapted to use linen and hemp rag rather than mulberry bark. It made the written word cheap enough to build a civilisation of books on.
entries.note: Bloom, 'Paper Before Print' (2001); the Talas story as tradition, the industry as fact.

entries.label: The Banu Musa and the Book of Ingenious Devices
entries.hint: The three sons of Musa ibn Shakir, patrons and geometers at al-Ma'mun's court, compiled the 'Kitab al-Hiyal' — a hundred devices using siphons, floats, valves and crank mechanisms, including automatic fountains, a self-trimming lamp and the earliest known feedback-control systems.
entries.note: Banu Musa, 'The Book of Ingenious Devices', trans. Hill (1979); the automation tradition continued by al-Jazari (13th c.).

entries.label: The astrolabe workshop
entries.hint: Abbasid instrument-makers turned the astrolabe from a rare Greek object into a standard, mass-produced brass computer for telling time, finding the qibla, and doing astronomy and astrology. Signed and dated examples survive from the 9th century onward.
entries.note: the earliest dated Islamic astrolabes; King, 'Astrolabes and Angels, Epigrams and Enigmas' (2007).

entries.label: The hospital as an institution
entries.loc: Baghdad (the Adudi came later; earlier the Barmakid and Muqtadiri hospitals)
entries.hint: The bimaristan — a purpose-built, endowed, staffed hospital with separate wards, an out-patient service, a pharmacy and a teaching function — was developed in Abbasid Baghdad, drawing on the older Persian model of Jundishapur, and became a fixture of every major Islamic city.
entries.note: Pormann & Savage-Smith, 'Medieval Islamic Medicine' (2007); the Muqtadiri hospital (founded 918).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Greek science into Arabic, an embassy to Charlemagne, Ibn Fadlan on the Volga, and three rival caliphs

entries.label: The Christian and Sabian translators
entries.hint: The Greek sciences reached Arabic largely through non-Muslims: Nestorian Christians like Hunayn ibn Ishaq and his family, who worked from Syriac versions, and the star-worshipping Sabians of Harran like Thabit ibn Qurra, who brought a living Greek mathematical tradition. Confessional boundaries did not bound the enterprise.
entries.note: Hunayn's own 'Risala' listing his Galen translations; Gutas (1998); the Harran Sabians (van Bladel, 'The Arabic Hermes', 2009).

entries.label: Harun al-Rashid and Charlemagne
entries.hint: Frankish and Abbasid embassies exchanged gifts — a water-clock, an elephant named Abul-Abbas, keys to the Holy Sepulchre. The contact was real but minor for Baghdad and large for the Franks; it fixed the image of Harun's court in the European imagination.
entries.note: the Frankish annals (Einhard; the Royal Frankish Annals); the Arabic sources are silent, which is itself informative (Borrut; Nelson, 'King and Emperor', 2019).

entries.label: Ibn Fadlan on the Volga
entries.loc: Baghdad to Bulgar, on the middle Volga
entries.hint: The caliph al-Muqtadir sent an embassy to the recently converted king of the Volga Bulgars. Its secretary Ibn Fadlan wrote a report describing the Turks, the Bashkirs and, most famously, a Rus chieftain's ship-cremation funeral — the fullest eyewitness account of the 10th-century north.
entries.note: Ibn Fadlan, 'Risala', trans. Lunde & Stone, 'Ibn Fadlan and the Land of Darkness' (2012).

entries.label: Manuscript-hunting in Byzantium
entries.hint: Abbasid missions to Byzantium came back with Greek manuscripts as much as with treaties, and the demand may have helped spark the 9th-century Byzantine revival of classical learning. Two civilisations that fought every summer were, in the libraries, feeding each other.
entries.note: the accounts of manuscript acquisition (al-Nadim's 'Fihrist'); the debated link to the 'first Byzantine humanism' (Lemerle).

entries.label: Three caliphs at once
entries.hint: The Fatimid leader took the title of caliph in Ifriqiya in 909; the Umayyad ruler of al-Andalus answered with his own claim in 929. For the first time three men called themselves the sole legitimate leader of all Muslims simultaneously. The idea of one caliphate survived only as an ideal.
entries.note: Halm, 'The Empire of the Mahdi' (1996); the Córdoban claim (see the Al-Andalus 711–1031 folio). Cross-references the Qarmatian entries.

entries.label: The Darb Zubayda — the pilgrim road
entries.hint: Harun's wife Zubayda paid for the paving, milestones, wells and cisterns of the pilgrim road from Iraq to Mecca, and a water supply for Mecca itself. The Hajj was the largest regular movement of people in the medieval world, and the Abbasids ran it as a showpiece of the caliph's care for the umma.
entries.note: the Darb Zubayda (Saudi archaeological survey; al-Rashid, 'Darb Zubaydah', 1980).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Persianisation at the centre, fragmentation at the edges, slave armies, and the Buyids at the door

entries.label: The Sasanian model revived
entries.hint: With the centre in Iraq and the state run by Persian secretaries, the caliphate absorbed the political culture of the empire it had replaced: the vizier, elaborate court ceremonial, the veil between ruler and subject, the genre of advice-literature for kings, the Persian new-year at court.
entries.note: the 'Sasanian revival' (Gutas 1998, ch. 2; Marlow, 'Hierarchy and Egalitarianism in Islamic Thought', 1997).

entries.label: The provinces slip away
entries.hint: Governors turned their offices into hereditary dynasties while still sending the Friday prayer in the caliph's name: the Aghlabids in Tunisia (800), the Tahirids and then Saffarids and Samanids in the east, the Tulunids in Egypt (868). The caliphate became a confederation of autonomous states around a symbolic centre.
entries.note: Kennedy, 'The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates' (2016), part 3; the 'dynasties' surveyed in Bosworth, 'The New Islamic Dynasties' (1996).

entries.label: The slave-soldier state
entries.hint: Al-Mu'tasim's decision to build his army from enslaved Turks bought from beyond the frontier created a self-reproducing military caste with no roots in the society it ruled. The pattern — the mamluk or ghulam army — became the normal way Islamic states raised troops for the next thousand years, and the Samarra anarchy was its first breakdown.
entries.note: Gordon, 'The Breaking of a Thousand Swords' (2001); Pipes, 'Slave Soldiers and Islam' (1981); Crone, 'Slaves on Horses' (1980).

entries.label: Byzantium turns the tide
entries.hint: After Lalakaon in 863 the initiative on the eastern frontier passed to Byzantium. The Macedonian emperors pushed the border east, and by the 940s the reconquests of Crete, Cilicia and Antioch were in sight — while the caliphate could no longer field an army to stop them.
entries.note: Treadgold, 'A History of the Byzantine State and Society' (1997); the frontier reversal.

entries.label: The Buyids take Baghdad
entries.hint: Ahmad ibn Buya, a Daylamite soldier from the Caspian highlands leading a Shia dynasty, marched into Baghdad and took over. He left the Abbasid caliph on his throne, drawing a pension and lending legitimacy, and ran the state himself with the title 'commander of commanders'. The caliphate had stopped being a government.
entries.note: Miskawayh, 'Tajarib al-Umam'; Busse, 'Chalif und Grosskönig: Die Buyiden im Iraq' (1969); Kraemer, 'Humanism in the Renaissance of Islam' (1986). Continued in the next folio.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The Turkish soldier-slaves, the singing-girls, the women who ran the palace, and a mystic on the gallows

entries.label: The ghilman — enslaved soldiers who ruled
entries.hint: Bought as boys from the Turkish steppe, converted, trained together and manumitted into the army, the ghilman owed everything to their commanders and nothing to the society around them. Within thirty years they were choosing and killing caliphs. It was a new kind of person in Islamic politics — unfree in origin, sovereign in fact.
entries.note: Gordon, 'The Breaking of a Thousand Swords' (2001); the ghulam institution (Crone, 'Slaves on Horses', 1980).

entries.label: The qiyan — the singing-girls as an institution
entries.hint: Trained from childhood in poetry, music and repartee and sold for enormous sums, the qiyan were the most cultivated women of the age and, through the men who competed for them, wielded real influence. Some — Arib, Inan, Mahbuba — became famous poets and composers; the childbearing route could make one an umm walad and then free.
entries.note: al-Jahiz, 'Risalat al-Qiyan' (trans. Beeston, 1980); Kitab al-Aghani; Caswell, 'The Slave Girls of Baghdad' (2011).

entries.label: The women who ran the palace
entries.hint: Khayzuran, Harun's mother and a former slave, was effectively co-ruler in the 780s; Zubayda funded the pilgrim road and a water supply for Mecca; and Shaghab, mother of al-Muqtadir, with her stewardess and her qahramana officials, directed the government for much of 908–932. The harem was a department of state.
entries.note: al-Tabari; Abbott, 'Two Queens of Baghdad' (1946); El Cheikh, 'Women, Islam, and Abbasid Identity' (2015).

entries.label: The many slaveries of the Abbasid world
entries.hint: Abbasid slavery was not one condition but several: the East African Zanj worked to death in gangs on the salt flats; the Turkish ghilman rose to command armies; the qiyan and the eunuch chamberlains lived at the centre of power; the saqaliba came the length of Europe. Legal status and lived reality could not have been further apart.
entries.note: the range of servile roles (Marmon, ed., 'Slavery in the Islamic Middle East', 1999); the Zanj (Popovic 1999). Cross-references the Zanj Revolt entry.

entries.label: The People of the Book as a professional elite
entries.hint: For all the legal subordination of the dhimma, Christians dominated medicine and translation, Jews a good part of banking and long-distance trade, and both supplied secretaries to the diwans. The Nestorian catholicos and the Jewish exilarch were installed by the caliph and answered to him — subordinate, but woven into the state.
entries.note: Fiey, 'Chrétiens syriaques sous les Abbassides' (1980); Fischel (1937); Griffith, 'The Church in the Shadow of the Mosque' (2008).

entries.label: Al-Hallaj and the limits of religious expression
entries.hint: The Sufi al-Hallaj preached in the streets, claimed union with God in words that sounded like a claim to be God, and was flogged, mutilated and hanged after an eleven-year trial in which political and doctrinal charges were tangled together. His execution marked the boundary the scholars would police between mysticism and heresy.
entries.note: Massignon, 'The Passion of al-Hallaj: Mystic and Martyr of Islam' (1922; Eng. 1982); the trial documents in the Arabic sources.
